content: Oil of guaiac is a fragrant substance commonly utilized in the production of soap. It is derived from the palo santo tree, scientifically known as Bulnesia sarmientoi. The oil is obtained through the process of steam distillation, which involves a mixture of wood and sawdust from the palo santo tree. Despite its name, it is sometimes mistakenly referred to as guaiac wood concrete. This substance appears as a yellow to greenish-yellow semi-solid mass, which has a melting point of approximately 40–50°C. Once melted, it can be cooled back to room temperature and remain in a liquid state for an extended period. The oil possesses a delicate, rose-like fragrance, reminiscent of the scent of hybrid tea roses or violets. Due to this similarity, it has occasionally been used as an adulterant for rose oil. The primary chemical composition of oil of guaiac includes 42–72% guaiol, along with other compounds such as bulnesol, d-bulnesene, b-bulnesene, a-guaiene, guaioxide, and b-patchoulene. It is considered safe for human skin, as it is non-irritating, non-sensitizing, and non-phototoxic. Historically, oil of guaiac was employed as a remedy for syphilis during the pre-Renaissance period.
